code.title: JS engine vs runtime: what exists where

followUps:
No. setTimeout belongs to the runtime (the host), not to the ECMAScript language. Browsers define it in the HTML specification and Node.js implements its own version. A bare engine such as V8's d8 shell may not have it at all.

The language only defines promise jobs; timers and the event loop come from the host. That is why setTimeout returns a number in browsers but a Timeout object in Node.

Stick to language features and put every host-specific call behind a small wrapper that you pick by feature detection.

Use typeof window !== "undefined" or globalThis to detect the host, never read document or process directly. Prefer APIs that now exist in both, such as fetch, URL, TextEncoder, structuredClone and ES modules.

const read = typeof process !== "undefined"
  ? (p) => require("fs").readFileSync(p, "utf8")
  : (p) => fetch(p).then((r) => r.text());

code.title: var, let and const: scope, hoisting, TDZ

followUps:
The TDZ (Temporal Dead Zone) is the stretch from entering a scope until the line that declares a let or const, during which touching the name throws a ReferenceError.

It was introduced with ES2015 so that using a variable before it is set is a loud error instead of a silent undefined (the var behaviour), and so const can never be observed without its value. Example: { console.log(x); let x = 1; } throws, while the same with var prints undefined. It is "temporal" because it depends on time of execution, not position in the text.

Call Object.freeze, but know that it is shallow, so nested objects must be frozen too.

const only stops reassigning the name. Object.freeze(o) makes the properties of o read-only (writes are ignored, or throw in strict mode). Inner objects stay mutable, so freeze recursively.

function deepFreeze(o) {
  Object.values(o).forEach(v => {
    if (typeof v === "object" && v !== null) deepFreeze(v);
  });
  return Object.freeze(o);
}

Cost is O(n) over all nested values. TypeScript's as const or readonly only checks at compile time.

code.title: The eight data types and typeof

followUps:
Use Array.isArray(x). It is the only check that is both correct and works across frames.

typeof [] is just "object", so it cannot tell arrays from other objects. x instanceof Array fails when the array came from another iframe or realm, because that realm has its own Array constructor. Array.isArray([]) is true, Array.isArray({length: 0}) is false, and Array.isArray(new Uint8Array(2)) is false too.

Because JavaScript temporarily wraps the primitive in an object when you use a property on it. After the call the wrapper is thrown away.

For "abc".toUpperCase() the engine creates a temporary String object, finds toUpperCase on String.prototype, calls it and returns the primitive "ABC". This is why "abc".length is 3 but "abc".x = 1 is lost (a TypeError in strict mode): the wrapper that held x no longer exists. The primitive itself stays unchanged.

code.title: null vs undefined

followUps:
They use different rules: the relational operators convert null to a number, but == has a special rule that null equals only null and undefined.

null >= 0 becomes 0 >= 0, which is true. null > 0 is false and null < 0 is false. But null == 0 never converts, so it is false. The result is that null is neither less than, greater than nor equal to 0, yet it is greater-or-equal. Avoid relying on this: check for null explicitly first.

Return null when you know the answer and it is "nothing"; use undefined when the value was not provided or does not exist.

In JSON, null survives while undefined fields are dropped, so {"nickname": null} tells the client "checked, empty" and a missing key means "unknown". Default parameters also react only to undefined: f(null) does not use the default. Pick one convention per API and document it, e.g. find() returns undefined (like Array.prototype.find) but a database column with no value is null.

code.title: == vs === coercion table

followUps:
Follow the conversions one at a time; the result is true.

  1. ![]: an array is truthy, so ![] is false. Now it is [] == false.
  2. A boolean becomes a number: [] == 0.
  3. The object becomes a primitive: [].toString() is "", so "" == 0.
  4. The string becomes a number: 0 == 0, which is true.

That is why [] == ![] is true even though [] is truthy.

includes and Map keys use SameValueZero, while indexOf uses strict equality (===).

The difference only shows for NaN: [NaN].includes(NaN) is true, [NaN].indexOf(NaN) is -1. SameValueZero treats NaN as equal to itself and +0 as equal to -0. Object.is is stricter still and separates +0 from -0. Objects always compare by reference in all of these, so new Map().set({}, 1).get({}) is undefined.

code.title: Falsy and truthy values

followUps:
It converts a value to a real boolean by applying ! twice: the first ! flips the truthiness, the second flips it back. It is the same as Boolean(x).

Examples: !!"0" is true, !!0 is false, !![] is true. It is useful when you must return or store a boolean, such as return !!user.token;. You do not need it inside if or while, which already apply the conversion.

document.all is an old Internet Explorer feature that is deliberately falsy, though it is an object.

It is the only object with this behaviour: typeof document.all is "undefined", Boolean(document.all) is false and document.all == null is true. The spec calls this the [[IsHTMLDDA]] internal slot. Browsers kept it so old scripts that wrote if (document.all) to detect IE would keep working. It is why "exactly eight falsy values" is true for the language but browsers add this one host object.

code.title: Floating point and money in cents

followUps:
It is 2^53 - 1 = 9007199254740991, the largest integer that doubles can always store exactly.

A double has 53 significant bits (52 stored plus one implied). Up to 2^53 every integer fits. Beyond it, the gap between neighbouring doubles is 2, so some integers cannot be represented. For example 9007199254740992 === 9007199254740993 is true. The "minus 1" is because 2^53 + 1 is not exact, so 2^53 - 1 is the largest value where it and its neighbours are all unique and exact. Test with Number.isSafeInteger(n); use BigInt beyond it.

Because 1.005 is actually stored as a number slightly below it, about 1.00499999999999989, so rounding to 2 decimals gives 1.00.

toFixed rounds the exact stored binary value, not the decimal text you typed. Multiplying does not help: 1.005 * 100 is 100.49999999999999. Safer options: keep money in integer cents, or round using the decimal string trick Number(Math.round("1.005e2") + "e-2"), which gives 1.01 because "1.005e2" is parsed exactly as 100.5.

code.title: NaN and isNaN vs Number.isNaN

followUps:
They use different equality: includes uses SameValueZero, which says NaN equals NaN, while indexOf uses ===, where NaN !== NaN.

So [NaN].includes(NaN) is true and [NaN].indexOf(NaN) is -1. If you need the position of a NaN, use a predicate: [1, NaN].findIndex(Number.isNaN) gives 1. Both methods scan the array, O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

Find where the first NaN appears, since it then spreads to everything it touches.

  1. Check inputs at the boundary: Number.isFinite(x) catches NaN and Infinity.
  2. Log or assert after each stage and bisect to the first bad step.
  3. Look for typical sources: parseInt(undefined), undefined + 1, 0/0, Infinity - Infinity, a missing object field.
function num(x, label) {
  if (!Number.isFinite(x)) throw new Error(label + " is " + x);
  return x;
}

Cost is O(1) per check.

code.title: How + chooses concatenation or addition

followUps:
[] + [] is "", [] + {} is "[object Object]", and a leading {} + [] is 0 in older consoles.

Both arrays become "" (an empty join) and a plain object becomes "[object Object]", so the first two are string concatenation. At the start of a statement, {} is parsed as an empty block, so what is left is the unary +[], which is +"", i.e. 0. Wrapped as ({} + []) or assigned to a variable it is "[object Object]". Modern DevTools often wrap input, hiding this.

Date is the exception: with + it behaves like a string, but with - like a number.

For the default hint, Date's Symbol.toPrimitive chooses string. So new Date(0) + 1 gives something like "Thu Jan 01 1970 ... 1" (concatenation), while new Date(5) - new Date(2) is 3 (milliseconds). To get the timestamp use +date or date.getTime(), and date1 - date2 for a duration.

code.title: || vs ?? and logical assignment

followUps:
Because obj.x ??= 1 only assigns when obj.x is null or undefined, while obj.x = obj.x ?? 1 always writes.

The logical assignment short-circuits: if x already has a value, nothing is written and no setter runs. The long form still performs the assignment, which calls a setter, can trigger a Proxy trap and throws a TypeError in strict mode on a frozen or read-only property even when the value is unchanged. For Object.freeze({x: 5}), obj.x ??= 1 is fine, but obj.x = obj.x ?? 1 throws in strict mode.

Use optional chaining: user?.profile?.name.

Each ?. stops and returns undefined if the thing on its left is null or undefined. Add a default with ??: user?.profile?.name ?? "anonymous". One difference: the old && chain also stops on falsy values such as 0 or "" and returns them, while ?. only guards null and undefined. For example with user = {profile: ""} the old form returns "" and the new form returns undefined for .name's access result of an empty string.

code.title: Automatic semicolon insertion pitfalls

followUps:
StandardJS and the standard style (and Prettier with semi: false) skip semicolons; Airbnb and Google style require them. The no-semicolon rule is to start any line that begins with (, [ or a backtick with a leading ;.

Those are the only characters where ASI does not insert anything, so ;[1, 2].forEach(f) is safe. Also never put a line break after return, break, continue or throw. A linter (no-unexpected-multiline) catches the rest.

Because ++ and -- are restricted productions: a postfix operator must be on the same line as its operand, so a newline stops it from attaching to a.

The parser inserts a semicolon and reads a; ++b, where ++ is now a prefix operator on b. With a = 1, b = 1 the result is a = 1, b = 2. The same rule is behind the return newline bug.

code.title: UTF-16 strings, code points and graphemes

followUps:
Count graphemes (what a user sees as one character) with Intl.Segmenter and cut after 280 of them, not by length or slice.

const seg = new Intl.Segmenter("en", {granularity: "grapheme"});
const parts = [...seg.segment(text)];
const cut = parts.slice(0, 280)
  .map(p => p.segment).join("");

text.slice(0, 280) may cut a surrogate pair or a family emoji in half. A family emoji is 8 UTF-16 units but one grapheme. Cost is O(n) time and space. Note that real services often use their own weighted counting rules, so confirm what limit is required.

They check for and repair lone surrogates, which are half of an emoji pair with no partner and make the string invalid Unicode (ES2024).

"\uD800".isWellFormed() is false; "\uD800".toWellFormed() returns "\uFFFD", the replacement character. This matters because functions like encodeURIComponent throw a URIError on a lone surrogate, and encoding such text to UTF-8 would be lossy. A typical cause is slicing a string through the middle of an emoji with slice.

code.title: Legacy quirks: typeof null and strict mode

followUps:
Strict mode ("use strict") turns several silent mistakes into errors and removes a few unsafe features.

  1. Assigning to an undeclared name throws a ReferenceError instead of creating a global.
  2. this in a plain function call is undefined, not the global object.
  3. Writing to a read-only or frozen property throws a TypeError.
  4. Duplicate parameter names, the with statement and octal literals like 010 are syntax errors.

ES modules and classes are strict by default.

TC39 is the committee that standardises JavaScript, and every proposal moves through numbered stages, each needing the committee's consensus.

  • Stage 0: an idea.
  • Stage 1: a proposal with a champion and a described problem.
  • Stage 2: draft with spec text.
  • Stage 2.7: approved design, needs tests.
  • Stage 3: candidate, browsers implement and give feedback.
  • Stage 4: finished, with tests and two shipping implementations, and included in the next yearly ECMAScript edition.

code.title: Money and big IDs: integer cents, string IDs

followUps:
Store each amount as an integer in the currency's smallest unit together with its number of decimal places, and never assume 2.

ISO 4217 says JPY has 0 decimals and KWD has 3. So 1,500 yen is stored as 1500 (exponent 0) and 1.250 KWD as 1250 (exponent 3). Keep a table or ask Intl.NumberFormat for resolvedOptions().maximumFractionDigits. Convert for display only: minor / 10 ** digits. Some currencies also have cash rounding rules (for example to 0.05), so keep that separate from storage.

Round once per defined step, in integer minor units, using one documented rule, and apply the same rule everywhere (client, server, reports).

The usual choice is to round each line item, then sum the lines, because the printed lines must add up to the printed total. Be aware that this can differ from rounding the whole sum. Example: three lines of 333 cents with a 10% discount: each is 299.7, rounded to 300, total 900. Rounding the sum instead gives 999 * 0.9 = 899.1, i.e. 899. Pick the rule your tax law or contract specifies, and test with such cases.
